notes.text: Who is working for Amazon Mechanical Turk?

Amazon Mechanical Turk is a marketplace for paid microtasks, introduced in 2005 and named after the 18th century chess automaton that appeared autonomous while a human operator was hidden inside the cabinet.
The machine seemed intelligent but intelligence and labour was concealed.
On the platform, individuals complete small units of work that machines cannot yet perform. Much of this work contributes to the creation of datasets used to train machine learning systems.
Image tagging. Transcription. Categorization. Short descriptions. Moderation.
Repetitive actions compensated in cents.
To understand how this operates from within, I decided to create an account as a requester.
That allowed me to define instructions, set payment, and decide what would count as acceptable work.
I started by asking for a photograph of the view from outside the window. I offered $0.20.
Before posting the request, I watched YouTube tutorials and read Reddit threads where workers exchange strategies.
Most conversations were practical: how to avoid rejection, how to calculate hourly return, how to recognize unreliable requesters.
Workers often report earning between $1 and $6 per hour.

Because the platform does not allow direct image uploads, I structured the request through a Google Form. The form allowed participants to upload a photo, write their city of origin, and include their MTurk ID.
After completing it, they received a code to enter back into the platform and claim the reward.
With this round, I collected 203 pictures. The initial goal had been 100.
More than 50% of the images did not comply with the request. Some files were broken. Others were desktop screenshots, stock photographs, or unrelated images.
Several entries were duplicated, sometimes more than once.
At first glance this appears as unusable material. But it also reflects how workers navigate a system where payment is low and review is uncertain.
Submitting quickly can reduce exposure. Reusing an image reduces effort. Duplicating an entry increases the probability of payment.
These gestures are not loud refusals. They are adjustments inside constraints. A form of micro-resistance embedded in routine practice.
Among the compliant images were residential streets, parking lots, fragments of sky, and apartment buildings.
In several photographs there were intimate details: a curtain pulled aside by a hand, a timestamp showing 4am on a monitor, the reflections of the photographer on a glass.
I asked for a view outward. The images also revealed the interior.
Each submission appeared in my dashboard as a single row with two options: approve or reject.
Approval transferred money. Rejection withheld it.
In both cases, the file remained accessible to me.
The material does not disappear when payment is refused. The archive expands regardless.
More than one year later, I returned to the platform and asked for photographs of working setups.
I uploaded my own desk as a reference image.
The first submission I received was the same image.
The next submission was identical.
Then it appeared again.
The example became the dominant response.
I asked for 100 images and received 140.
Submitting the example requires no additional effort.
By default, submissions are automatically approved after a couple of days unless manually reviewed. Workers know this. They understand that scale makes detailed review unlikely.
With a few hundred entries, I can still check one by one. At a larger scale, attention shifts to metrics.
The interface reduces each submission to a binary decision.
Approve. Reject.
Yet each image carries traces that exceed the instruction: open tabs, background applications, battery level, the type of computer, and glimpses of the room in which the work is taking place.
A bed behind the desk. A kitchen table used as a workstation. Night visible through a window.
These elements are incidental, but they reveal conditions of labor. When datasets are cleaned, these traces are removed. Here they remain visible.
The image of a desk becomes more than documentation of a workspace. It becomes a fragment of domestic space entangled with digital piecework.
After collecting windows and desks, I asked workers what they like and detest about working on the platform and why they continue.
I posted the prompt twice. Once open to all workers. Once restricted to workers with Master status.
The open round was completed in less than one hour.
The Masters round remained active for three days and closed with 17 responses.
Master status is assigned and maintained through continuous performance monitoring.

One worker wrote: 
 "On one hand, mturk changed my life. I have C-PTSD and find public places too noisy and stressful. I was on the verge of becoming completely homeless but went back to working on here. It now gives me a chance to earn enough money to survive. On the other hand, it's a terrible way to make a living. It's not stable and can be stressful."

Another wrote:
  "Amazon plays no role in defending the worker."

Several described unexplained rejections, technical malfunctions, and unpaid time. Some expressed anxiety about maintaining approval rates above strict thresholds required to access better-paying assignments.
Access to work depends on percentages. Percentages depend on judgments that are rarely explained.
Workers are aware of this. They share information on forums. They warn each other about unreliable requesters. They decide which assignments to avoid.
What appears as flexibility often reads, in these testimonies, as dependency and risk management.
This is visible in many answers.

"Amazon Mechanical Turk HIT jobs can be a great source of extra income for those with full-time or part-time job" 
 A safe answer. The tone is positive and careful.
A safe answer. The tone is positive and careful.
The same interface that allows me to reject submissions structures how workers respond. They write carefully. They anticipate evaluation. They adjust their tone.
I selected the window photographs and uploaded them again, asking workers to describe what they saw.
Hundreds of descriptions arrived in less than one hour.
I then uploaded those descriptions and asked other workers to produce drawings based solely on the written text.
The sequence was simple: image, text, drawing.
Some descriptions were detailed paragraphs. Others were short. Some consisted only of tags.
Houses and trees. NICE PHOTO. A bike and some trees. GARDEN. car.
When asked to draw, several workers did not draw. They wrote the description again. Others reduced the scene to recognizable objects.
Cars. Bus. People. Tree.
This does not necessarily indicate misunderstanding. It reflects how work on the platform is structured.
Workers are repeatedly asked to identify and confirm objects. Drawing is not a common or rewarded task. Labeling is.
Instead of adapting to an unfamiliar instruction, some translated it into a format that is legible within the system.
With each step, context narrowed. The atmosphere faded. Spatial relations disappeared. The scene became extractable elements.
This transformation follows the logic of the platform.
Between image and label something is removed.
That removal is structural.
Across windows, desks, and written testimonies, the same pattern is visible.
People adapt. They adjust. They reuse. They simplify. They resist in small ways.
The platform appears automated.
Inside it, labor is fragmented, distributed, and constantly recalibrated.
And within that recalibration, there is not only compliance, but agency.
